messages.subject: Problems Defining a Nimble Model
messages.body_plain:
I have implemented a Stan program to calculate the rate constants in a simple iodine pharmacokinetic model (see bottom of attached file). I am trying to solve the same problem in Nimble (using the eigensystem rather than the matrix exponential to solve the ODE's) but in the nimbleCode step I get the error

Error in genVarInfo3() : Dimension of kt is 1, which does not match its usage in 'm[i] <- q.thy(t.b[i], kt)'.

which I don't understand. I would appreciate some clarification on the nature of my error and some advice on how to resolve the problem.

Tom

messages.body_plain:
Nimble *model code* is particularly sensitive to indexing, and generally requires "full indexing" to be provided for any non-scalars appearing in the model code.

e.g., see model code below, which works fine now:

modelA <- nimbleCode( {
  kt[1] ~ dlnorm(log(0.9336),log(1.25))
  kt[2] ~ dlnorm(log(1.92),log(1.25))
  kt[3] ~ dlnorm(log(0.004992),log(1.25))
  kt[4] ~ dlnorm(log(0.05328),log(1.25))
  kt[5] ~ dlnorm(log(0.008736),log(1.25))
  beta ~ dlnorm(log(2000),log(3))
  Q ~ T(dnorm(1,sd=2),1,)
  for (i in 1:37) {
    m[i] <- q.thy(t.b[i],kt[1:5])    ## "full indexing" now provided on kt[1:5]
    M[i] ~ dnorm(beta*m[i],sd=Q*u[i])
  }
})

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Aha, thanks.

I can't follow the type declarations in your code.  It looks like you've got this figured out, but just to be sure, in nimble's type-declaration system, "double(0)" means scalar and "double(1)" means vector.

In the line

m[i] <- q.thy(t.b[i],kt[1:5])

It looks like you want q.thy to take a scalar and vector for the first and second argument, respectively, and to return a scalar.

The code for q.thy declares a vector for the first argument (x) and for the returnType.  That's inconsistent with how you use it in the model.  You could change those to scalars, but the problem runs another layer deeper.  q.thy calls q.es <http://q.es>, passing x as the second argument, and in q.es <http://q.es> it looks like you really do want x to be a vector.  That's why I can't follow your intent here.  You pass scalar element t.b[i] into what is expected to be a vector (x) and the code q.thy code eventually (in q.es <http://q.es>) tries to use it as a vector.

I am not sure, but you might want the following.  If q.thy should really take x as a vector and return m as a vector, you would use

m[1:37] <- q.thy(t.b[1:37], kt[1:5])

This would create a vector node m of length 37 (not in the for loop).

If I've missed the boat, can you explain what you need?

-Perry

messages.subject: Re: Comparing eigen to nimEigen
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tom, in general, in nimbleFunction code, we use the Eigen C++ package for linear algebra, so nimEigen uses Eigen. In contrast R's eigen uses LAPACK. So there may be numerical differences between Eigen and LAPACK for a given matrix.

For k.bad, it seems that LAPACK and Eigen give the same result.

For the transpose of k.bad, it appears there are numerical differences between LAPACK and Eigen. The result from Eigen has non-zero imaginary parts for the 4th and 5th eigenvalues, but those imaginary parts are very small (around 5 x 10^-18). NIMBLE doesn't handle complex numbers so in post-processing of the Eigen output, we turn the complex values into NaN values.

I'll file an issue for our development team so that we consider returning the real part in such cases where the imaginary part is negligible.

hi Alison,

We don't have any specific plans to add this functionality, partly as this is the sort of thing you can code in NIMBLE via a user-defined function
or user-defined distribution (which of these will depend on the details of how you implement things) and then use that function in your model code.
For the 'pred' functions you'd need to write out some matrix algebra code to do the prediction given a multivariate normal specified for the
"training" locations where you have information.

look at modules/user_dist_gaussproc.Rmd file.

If you try to go the route of writing user-defined functions/distributions and would like more specific tips, please feel free to follow up here.
And if you or anyone else does code up any of these and want to share, we'd be happy to help share / publicize what you develop.

Chris

messages.subject: Re: WAIC caculate as NAN
messages.body_plain:
Yes, if you're not monitoring the latent states in your model, then in some cases the WAIC calculation can end up as NaN.  But another reason it might be NaN, I'll caution, is that the MCMC is not operating properly on your model, for whatever reason.  This second problem you could diagnose by looking at traceplots of all sampled nodes, and making sure they're all "transitioning".  If any are "flatline", then they're not updating, and WAIC will be NaN (but the bigger problem: the MCMC is not updating some model parameters).

To add monitors for latent states, assuming you have the model object "Rmodel", and an MCMC configuration object "conf", you could use these lines:

nodesToMonitor <- Rmodel$getNodeNames(stochOnly = TRUE, includeData = FALSE)
conf$addMonitors(nodesToMonitor)

This will add monitors to the configuration object for *all* stochastic model nodes, which aren't designated as fixed data.  In particular, these will also include latent states in your model.

Then, continue to use the "conf" object to build the MCMC algorithm, compile, and run.

Hope this helps.

Daniel

messages.subject: Maximum a posteriori with NIMBLE
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I spoke with Chris last week about the possibility of using NIMBLE to maximise the log posterior for maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation, e.g. for initialising a complicated MCMC model.

I have come up with a simple working example, where I have written a function that overwrites the parameter values in the compiled NIMBLE model and runs calculate():

n <- 100
mu <- 4
sigma <- 1
y <- rnorm(100,mu,sigma)

map_code <- nimbleCode({
  for(i in 1:n){
    y[i] ~ dnorm(mu,sd=sigma)
  }
  mu ~ dnorm(0,sd=10)
  sigma ~ dexp(0.01)
})

map_constants <- list(n=n)
map_data <- list(y=y)

map_inits <- list(mu=3,sigma=4)

map_model <- nimbleModel(map_code,map_constants,map_data,map_inits)

map_compiled_model <- compileNimble(map_model)

map_lp <- nimbleFunction(run=function(x=double(1)){
  map_compiled_model$mu <- x[1]
  map_compiled_model$sigma <- x[2]
  return(-map_compiled_model$calculate())
})

nlm(map_lp,c(3,4))

In this example, I have two parameters mu and sigma which I overwrite individually. My question is, for more complicated models, is there an easy way to access / overwrite all of the parameter values in one go? I understand this might be challenging owing to issues such as unique dimensions between parameters, but I'm just interested if there is already a way of doing this, or if you can think of a quick workaround.

Best wishes,

Oliver

messages.subject: Re: Maximum a posteriori with NIMBLE
messages.body_plain:
Oliver, briefly, you're going to want to use the values() function.  It "flattens" all model variables, etc, down to vectors, so even if say 'a' is a scalar, 'b' is a vector, and 'X' is a matrix, then

nodes <- c('a', 'b', 'X')
values(model, nodes) <- [some vector of values of the correct length]

will work, and store new values for 'a', 'b', and 'X' into the model object.

You can also extract (a flattened vector of values) from a model, using values(), as:

valuesFromModel <- values(model, nodes)

The values (going into, or coming from) the model will be in the order in which the appear in the "nodes" vector, and matrices are "flattened" in columnwise ordering.

Another side note: it looks as though your map_lp nimbleFunction that you defined is missing a returnType() statement, namely:

returnType(double())

Without that, included as a standalone line in the run() function, I think it would fail compilation.

Good luck!  Keep at it!

Daniel
